source: Dutta, Ramachandran, Sra (2026) Active Inference as Context Acquisition for AI Agents
finding: First paper found that frames LLM question asking as expected free energy (risk + epistemic value + cost) and tests it against an exact dynamic-programming oracle. In deterministic tables the epistemic term equals expected information gain. Seven frontier models (GPT-5, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Grok 4) cut posterior entropy every turn but ask more questions than the oracle.
numbers: Binary tiers N=25 and 100 (Places, Cars, Animals); k-ary tiers N=100/200/300 with 8 attributes; 30 targets per tier; temperature 0; tools off. Planning gap = mean extra questions vs oracle; values are in figures only, not captured.
quote: In deterministic settings, the epistemic term reduces to expected information gain
limits: Enumerated attribute tables, noiseless truthful answers, uniform prior; the LLM chooses the question itself, EIG is not computed for it. Does not test EIG-ranked selection vs LLM choice. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean yardstick for S7: count questions to identify vs an optimal tree. Shows plain LLM test choice is still above optimal even on fully enumerated sets (gap 1, partial).

source: Dutta et al. (2026) Section 7: prompt autocompletion under token costs
finding: Entropy-per-token-cost question policy with a stop threshold raised constraint compliance. Asking nothing scored 0.0417 at about 112 tokens; the tuned weighted policy scored 0.375 at about 219 tokens. Epistemic value paid only for attributes the verifier checks.
numbers: 48 synthetic product tasks; 24 train and 24 held out for the grid search; best threshold 0.01 and Kmax=2; synthetic clarification costs 24/48/72 tokens; label-noise error rate 0.12; attribute weights hand set (format 1.0, length 0.6, tone 0.25).
quote: only when those questions buy information the final output will actually be judged on
limits: Simulated truthful answers, fixed templates, deterministic verifier that ignores tone; hand-set weights are a pragmatic term in disguise. No best-of-N control at 219 tokens. Small N.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 3: a goal-linked weight on information beats unweighted entropy only when it tracks what the final judge checks. For S7, weight tests by how much they matter to the final answer.

source: Dutta et al. (2026) Section 8: automated prompt optimization, EFE vs MI vs KG vs Thompson
finding: Six candidate system prompts treated as Bernoulli arms on ARC-Challenge. EFE was defined as a blend of mutual information and knowledge gradient with a linearly decaying epistemic weight, divided by token cost. Text says MI and EFE were most informative early; Thompson and round robin spread learning evenly; KG concentrated queries and left some prompts untested.
numbers: Cap 400 training questions (about 5e4 tokens; budget B=120,000); holdout accuracies shown in figure only, not captured.
limits: Qualitative reading of figures; one benchmark; the weight schedule is fixed (linear decay), not swept. Cannot tell if EFE beat Thompson.
agent_relevance: Supports a decaying epistemic weight (explore first, commit later) as a schedule for S7 to S8, but is not a measured win over simple baselines.

source: Dutta et al. (2026) Prop 3.3 and Appendix B: stopping rule and greedy vs optimal
finding: Derives a stop rule: collect more evidence only when expected information I(x;o|a) exceeds lambda times cost. States that greedy one-step EIG optimises only the immediate entropy drop, while the DP recursion is optimal for expected remaining questions. For larger tiers it suggests greedy EIG, shallow lookahead or sampling planners as baselines.
numbers: No empirical comparison of greedy vs lookahead in LLMs; exact DP feasible only for the released tier sizes.
limits: Theory only for the lookahead part; deterministic answers, uniform prior.
agent_relevance: Gives S7 a concrete test-stop rule (information per token vs threshold) and a note that greedy EIG is a fine default but not optimal (gaps 5 and 8, theory only).

source: Luo et al. (2026) PUMA: Know You Before You Speak (EFE action selection for LLM dialogue)
finding: First quantitative test found of an EFE objective (epistemic = expected posterior entropy, pragmatic = log preference of predicted outcome) choosing actions in an LLM agent, against baselines on a simulated counselling task. PUMA beat every baseline on all outcome measures with two 8B backbones.
numbers: CAMI simulator, Qwen3-8B: Lift 1.62, Prep 75.9%, TrigCov 62.4%, 12.2 turns, vs best baseline DIIR 1.07, 52.0%, 34.0%, 13.1 turns. Llama-3.1-8B: 1.76, 83.0%, 63.2%, 10.7 turns vs DIIR 1.17, 59.0%, 40.0%, 11.9 turns. CAMI-full 0.62/28% (Qwen).
limits: Client is an LLM simulator (DynPatient); judge is Qwen3-32B; PUMA also adds a learned world model and belief module, so the gain is not from EFE alone; no equal-token control; preprint, one task family.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 9 in part: a measured EFE-in-LLM result exists, but it is confounded with state modeling. Do not cite as proof that the EFE form beats plain information gain.

source: Luo et al. (2026) PUMA ablation Table 3 and fixed EFE weights
finding: Removing components lowered Lift by 0.17 to 0.28 from the full 1.62; removing both world model and EFE planning hurt most (Lift 1.35, Prep 55.2%, TrigCov 54.0%). Text says removing belief, world-model input or EFE selection each gave a comparable drop. Without world-model prediction the planner drifted to exploratory TrigCov (higher TrigCov, lower Lift). Epistemic and pragmatic weights fixed at 0.4 and 0.6; no weight sweep found in the text.
numbers: Lift drops -0.28, -0.21, -0.17, -0.21 across four ablation rows (row labels partly garbled in text extraction). Weights lambda_e=0.4, lambda_p=0.6, soft fusion 0.35.
limits: The epistemic term is entropy after the answer with a prior-entropy term dropped as constant; no epistemic-only or pragmatic-only ablation reported. Cannot locate a sweet spot.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open for the weight, but the one hint is that dropping planning lets the agent explore without making progress, which mirrors the Champion collapse in reverse.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks (NeurIPS D&B)
finding: On underspecified reasoning problems (exactly one missing variable), models pick the right clarifying question from a menu well on math but poorly on logic and planning. Chain of thought and few-shot gave no consistent gain. Ability to solve the fully specified problem did not predict ability to pick the right question.
numbers: Over 80% (GSM-Q, GSME-Q for best models) vs under 50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q (abstract says 40-50%). Breadth-first-search baseline reaches 39.0% (depth 3), 80.6% (depth 5), 99.8% (depth 10) on Logic-Q. Models: GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Gemma 2.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple-choice menu of questions, one missing variable; not EIG; models are 2024-vintage (Gemini 2.5 Pro examples are qualitative only). Per-cell table was garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 6 (math/logic): the hypotheses are 'which variable is missing', and implicit LLM choice is weak while a systematic search over the constraint graph is strong. Supports computing the test via search, not asking the model to guess it.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2024) Active Preference Inference using Language Models and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Inference-time method: LLM defines the conditional distributions of a small probabilistic model; sample 8 candidate questions, pick the one with lowest expected posterior entropy. Beats vanilla instruction-tuned LLM and ReAct on web-shopping preference inference using fewer questions. Expected entropy minimisation and expected model change are equivalent.
numbers: Surpasses both baselines after four questions with binary reward; also better with soft reward; exact percentages are in figures (not captured).
limits: Simplified shopping task with real products, simulated user; baselines are direct prompting, not a best-of-N control at equal tokens (the method uses extra LLM calls).
agent_relevance: Scaffold-only (no training) EIG selection works with LLM-defined likelihoods and an LLM-generated candidate list, so the hypothesis set need not be hand-built (gap 1, partial). Cost of the extra calls is not reported.

source: Andukuri, Franken, Gerstenberg, Goodman (2024) STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
finding: Rewards the questioner by the log-probability a gold response gets given the questions asked (an LLM-logprob estimate of information gain), then self-trains. After two iterations the questioner's final responses beat the initial model's in 72% of tasks. Training without regularisation reduced win rates.
numbers: 25,500 persona-task prompts; win rate 72% (GPT-4 judge, about 300 values per point); 65% with a weaker setup; 62% peak with gemma-7b roleplayer; llama3-8b version 66%; ablation with gold response in training converged to 50%.
limits: Training, not scaffold; simulated roleplayer; log-prob reward is a noisy proxy of EIG (gap 2).
agent_relevance: Shows LLM logprob of the outcome can serve as an information-gain signal and that unregularised optimisation of it degrades results. Reminds us to cap the number of tests (S7 budget).

source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough
finding: Base LLMs often overshoot or undershoot when deciding to stop asking questions or thinking. CaRT fine-tunes on counterfactual trajectory pairs (terminate vs continue) with a stated reason, improving success and efficiency in interactive diagnosis and math (AIME 2025). RL on top lengthened conversations.
numbers: Medical: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, 30 evaluation runs, 3 training runs, results in Pareto plots (numbers not captured). Math: Qwen3-1.7B traces, 2,000 DeepScaleR problems, 10 prefixes each.
limits: Fine-tuning, small models; comparisons are against the base model and SFT without counterfactuals; no prompt-only stop rule tested.
agent_relevance: Supports adding an explicit stop test to S7 (is the next test worth its cost) rather than trusting the model to stop. Partly addresses gap 8, but not the Bogdan CoT claim.

source: Gijsen, Grundei, Blankenburg (2022) Active inference and the two-step task, Sci Rep 12:17682
finding: Re-analysed four public two-step datasets, comparing an active inference model (EFE with information gain) against a hybrid RL model. Two datasets (Magic Carpet n=24, Spaceship n=21), which show more model-based behaviour and directed exploration, were better fit by active inference; the others fit about equally. About half of participants had a clearly nonzero information-gain weight. Exploration effects were only partly captured.
numbers: Datasets: Magic Carpet n=24, Spaceship n=21, Shock n=36, plus an online dataset. Family exceedance probabilities favoured active inference in the first two; BIC favoured it with some ambiguity; AIC and BIC disagreed on some model variants.
quote: approximately half of all participants showed sensitivity to information gain as formulated under active inference
limits: Fit advantage came partly from learning with probability distributions and belief decay, not only from the info-gain term; transition effects not fully reproduced. Compares reward-plus-info-gain vs RL, not EFE vs plain EIG.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 7: human choices are compatible with an information-gain term in about half of people, but pure EIG was not separated from EFE.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Neural correlates of novelty and variability in human decision-making under active inference, eLife
finding: Twenty-five participants did a contextual two-armed bandit with EEG. Active inference fit choices better than model-free and model-based RL. EFE was linked to frontal pole and middle frontal gyrus activity in source space.
numbers: N=25; model evidence favoured active inference (exact values in Figure 4c, not captured); reviewers asked for predictive checks, which the authors then added.
limits: Small N, one task; a plain information-bonus RL model was not in the comparison as far as the text shows; model fit is not a causal test.
agent_relevance: Keeps gap 7 mostly open: human behavioural fit exists but the key contrast (EFE vs EIG plus reward) was not run.

source: Nelson, McKenzie, Cottrell, Sejnowski (2010) Experience matters: information acquisition optimizes probability gain, Psychological Science
finding: Three experiments designed by computer optimisation to separate four value-of-information measures (information gain, KL distance, probability gain, impact). With experience-based learning of probabilities, probability gain (error minimisation) explained search better than information gain; the preference was robust in Experiment 3. Verbal summary statistics changed behaviour.
numbers: Three experiments; abstract does not give N. Only the abstract was opened (via Europe PMC).
quote: probability gain explained subjects' information search better than the other statistical theories or the probability-of-certainty heuristic
limits: Abstract only; older work and not framed as active inference; effect depends on how probabilities are learned.
agent_relevance: Strongest human data on which information measure people follow: probability gain, not Shannon EIG. Suggests testing probability-gain ranking as a cheaper S7 alternative.

source: Cogliati Dezza, Cleeremans, Alexander (2022) Independent and interacting value systems for reward and information in the human brain, eLife
finding: fMRI study finds two prefrontal regions that independently encode reward and information value. Fits EFE's two separate terms but also fits any two-term model.
numbers: 21 participants recruited, 20 analysed (one excluded for a structural scan problem).
limits: Small N; shows two signals exist, not that they are combined as EFE says.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping reward and information terms separate in S7 scoring (gap 7, weak).

source: Schwartenbeck, FitzGerald, Mathys, Dolan, Friston et al. (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration, eLife
finding: Simulations (100 to 1000 experiments of 32 trials) separate state-exploration (active inference) from parameter-exploration (active learning). Active inference fails in a learning task because it never samples the ambiguous option; it wins when the hidden context changes trial to trial. Reproduces monkey and bird findings qualitatively. No human data.
numbers: Simulated agents; 1000 experiments x 32 trials in Figure 6. First 100,000 characters of the page read.
limits: Simulation; authors note the two mechanisms may be hard to dissociate behaviourally.
agent_relevance: Warns that epistemic value over states alone misses the value of learning parameters; in S7 the hypothesis set must include model uncertainty, not just state uncertainty.

source: Mathar, Peters et al. (2025) Signatures of perseveration and heuristic-based directed exploration in two-step task behaviour
finding: Competing explanation to the EFE account of human data. An extended hybrid RL model with higher-order perseveration and a heuristic directed-exploration bonus fit best in two datasets, while a simpler model with perseveration alone was as good. Found a robust positive directed-exploration effect on stage-one choice.
numbers: Data 1: 39 men, 300 trials; Data 2: N=100 subsample of Gillan et al. 2016 online study.
limits: Not a test of EFE. Shows that a heuristic information bonus in RL explains the same kind of data that EFE models do.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: human data cannot separate EFE from an information bonus plus perseveration. Treat 'the brain does EFE' as unproven; use EIG for its engineering value only.

source: Active inference and artificial reasoning (2026), Sci Rep (PMC13601584), Friston-group structure learning with expected information gain
finding: Uses expected information gain over models, parameters and states to pick actions that disambiguate hypothesised rules (three-ball paradigm), using Bayesian model reduction. Removing gain over models and parameters raised mean discovery time from 19.4 to 28.5 trials and cut cumulative performance from 150 to 89.2. With no gain at all the Occam factor stayed near zero at trial 32.
numbers: 64 games with identical cue sequences with and without terms; two games undiscoverable without model-level gain; state-only gain gave one premature commitment (score 150 to 51).
limits: Simulation with small discrete models; not an LLM; no pragmatic-term weight sweep seen.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 analogue: EIG over candidate rules speeds hypothesis discovery by about a third in trials. Suggests S7 ranks tests by how they split competing explanations, not only by answer uncertainty.

source: Dutta et al. (2026) related-work map of LLM information-seeking methods (Hu 2024, Piriyakulkij 2023, Kobalczyk 2025, Choudhury 2025, Liu 2025)
finding: The newest paper in the area names Active Task Disambiguation and BED-LLM as the closest LLM Bayesian-experimental-design work and notes CaRT for termination. It cites no direct active-inference benchmark on LLM agents beyond its own, which suggests few exist.
limits: A citation map, not a systematic search; absence of papers is weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Supports the conclusion for gap 9 that EFE-labelled LLM work remains rare; most useful work calls itself Bayesian experimental design.

finding: arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned HTTP 429 for the whole session and the WebSearch budget ran out after one productive call, so no equal-token EIG vs LLM-choice comparison, no new estimator comparison and no replication of Bogdan could be located.
numbers: WebSearch: 1 productive call, then budget-exhausted. Europe PMC and direct arXiv PDF fetches worked.
limits: Absence of evidence here reflects tool limits, not a proven absence.
agent_relevance: Record gaps 1, 2, 4, 5, 8 as open with the partial evidence above.
